newsitem.title: FINLAND: FEATURE - Season ends fast for Finnish elk hunters.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Season ends fast for Finnish elk hunters.

text.p: Soon after dawn, a thick frost clinging to the shrubs and bracken on the forest floor, we are crouching behind huntsman Matti Nousiainen. Rifle cocked, he surveys his range.

We all wear red hats and jerkins, required by law for visibility. The Finns joke that "beneath a red cap there's always a red nose", but there is no alcohol to stave off the cold. Drinking, and a hot sauna, will come later.

We are on a hunt for elk -- the massive, heavy-antlered moose-like deer that roam the forests of the Nordic region. The hunt is a tradition born of need, especially in Finland's harsher northern areas.

"You can wait here for hours in the silence, watching," whispers Nousiainen, 59, and falls silent. Overhead in a blue autumn sky a flock of swans is beating its way south, away from the approaching winter.
A squall rips the leaves off a tree. In the quiet it sounds like a volley of pistol shots.
Then comes the real thing. The boom of a rifle in the range adjacent to ours. Nousiainen holds his breath.
Three more shots follow --confirmation of a kill, and a sign it is an adult stag.
Nousiainen shouts out the news.
"That's good," says Ari Pulkka, 32, our guide and interpreter, who does not hunt. "You're always worried the elk might be only injured."
After the shooting, as men gather around a forest bonfire, hunt leader Eero Savolainen tucks a sprig of fresh spruce into farmer Pentti Lyyra's red cap. It's a trophy, but the moment is bittersweet.
For the 13 men who call themselves "Viitaan Erapojat" or the Forest Boys of Viitaa, Lyyra's triumph means their hunting season, which could have lasted to mid-December, is over in just four hours.
The gentle 42-year-old just shot their quota -- one adult elk.
"It's the fifth I've ever got," he says, eyes shining. "Sometimes it takes forever, walking steadily for miles, waiting. This one just headed straight for me -- I got him in the chest."
Elsewhere elk hunting would be classified as a blood sport. But out here in the depths of central Finland nothing about this hunt seems gratuitous.

Whatever your opinion on the ethics of hunting -- or however squeamish city-dwellers feel about the gorier side of meat -- the elk-hunting ritual here is deeply ingrained, highly regulated, and still purposeful.

"There aren't so many elk around here at the moment," says Savolainen of his hunt's area, which spans a total of 2,000 to 3,000 hectares (5,000 to 7,500 acres). "So we only applied to kill one. To keep in practice."
Until relatively recently, fresh meat from the forest was vital nourishment to many Finns; for many the ability to live off and in the forest is still key to a deep sense of identity.
Ordinary Finns hunt elk. It has none of the slow spectacle of a bullfight or the pomp of a British fox hunt.
Elk are a problem. They eat young tree shoots and roam into the roads. To crash your car into an animal like the one here, which weighed perhaps 400 kg (880 lb), would mean certain death.
The day Pentti Lyyra shot this elk up in central Finland, two people were killed in just such a crash near the capital Helsinki. Their children, in the back of the car, were orphaned.
While the authorities rack their brains for clever ways to keep elk off the roads or warn drivers of the danger, hunting remains part of the solution.
This year throughout Finland, hunters have been licensed to shoot more than 20,000 elk. Finnish land law lets them travel freely over an agreed area, no matter who owns the land.
By the time we reach the spot where the elk fell, its throat has been cut and dark blood is steaming as it drains on to the green moss. Draining it fast gives the meat a better taste.
Soon, just with simple hunting knives, the men will empty the animal's guts on to the forest floor to feed other animals.

Waiting for a tractor to haul the carcass back to their lodge, the men around the bonfire joke, cook sausages and drink coffee, and talk about the party they will have. Around 200 people from the area will be invited to eat the meat.
"This elk was a bit stupid -- a bit young," says Lyyra. "An older one would know to keep under cover."

Elk move very fast. To earn a licence, these men must be able to get three shots on a static target within 20 seconds, and shoot a moving target three times within four and a half seconds as it zigzags over 25 metres (yards).
"That took some of us here quite a while," says Nousiainen, laughing: "Some of us were only used to shooting in the army."
Later at the lodge, as they share a bottle of whisky around the clean, hanging carcass, the Viitaa Forest Boys tell and re-tell the story and plan next week's big party.
"The whole village will get food, eat together, get meat," says Nousiainen. "It's a ritual for the end of summer."
